readings.head: {{RunningHeader|witted|6957|wizard}}
readings.c1s1:
¶
{{smaller block|The people be gentle, merry, quick and fine ''witted'', delighting in quietness, and, when need requireth, able to abide and suffer much bodily labour.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 7.}}
Renowned, ''witted'' Dulcimel, appeare.
{{right|''Marston'', The Fawne, v.}}}}

'''witter†''', ''a.'' [ME. ''witter'', ''witer'', < Icel. ''vitr'', knowing, < ''vita'', know: see ''wit''<sup>1</sup>.] Knowing; certain; sure.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tho wurth the child [Isaac] ''witter'' and war
That thor sal offrende ben don.</poem>
{{right|''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1308.}}}}

'''witter†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''witteren'', ''witeren'', < Icel. ''vitra'', make wise, make certain, < ''vitr'', knowing: see ''witter''.] To make sure; inform; declare (that).
{{smaller block|I ''witter'' the the emperour es entirde into Fraunce.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1239.}}}}

'''wittering†''', ''n.'' [ME., verbal n. of ''witter'', ''v.''] Information; knowledge.
{{smaller block|<poem>Leue Joseph, who tolde yow this?
How hadde ʒe ''wittering'' of this dede?</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 142.}}}}

'''witterly†''' (wit′ėr-li), ''adv.'' [ME.. also ''witterliche'', ''witerliche'', etc.; < ''witter'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Certainly; surely; truly.
{{smaller block|<poem>I blusshet hom on.
I waited hom ''witterly'', as me wele thoght,
All feturs in fere of the fre ladys.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2428.}}
Ful acorded was hit ''witterly''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 2606.}}}}

'''witters''', ''n. pl.'' See ''withers''.

'''witticaster''' (wit′i-kas-tėr), ''n.'' [< ''witty'' + ''-c-aster'' as in ''criticaster''.] An inferior or pretended wit.
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''wittol<sup>2</sup>''' (wit′ọl), ''n.'' A dialectal reduction of ''whitetail.'' [Cornwall, Eng.]

'''wittolly†''', ''a.'' [< ''wittol''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Like or characteristic of a wittol, or submissive cuckold. ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 2. 283.
{{smaller block|Her husband was hanged for his ''wittoldly'' permission, and shee herselfe drowned. ''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 293.}}

'''wit-tooth''' (wit′töth), ''n.'' A wisdom-tooth.

'''witts''' (wits), ''n. pl.'' Same as ''tin-wits.''
{{smaller block|When much pyrites [in tin-bearing rock] is present, it is necessary to make a preliminary concentration, and roast the enriched product (''witts'') in a furnace.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XVI. 466.}}}}

'''witty''' (wit′i), ''a.'' [< ME. ''witty'', ''wity'', ''witiȝ'', < AS. ''witig'', ''wittig'' (= OS. ''witig'' = OHG. ''wizzig'', MHG. ''witzec(g)'', G. ''witzig'' = Icel. ''vitugr'' = Sw. ''vitter'' = Dan. ''vittig''), knowing, wise, < ''wit'', knowledge, wit: see ''wit''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''witch''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' Possessed of wisdom or learning; wise; discreet; knowing; artful.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''wyttiour'' that eny wight is bote yf he worche ther-after,
The biterour he shal a-bygge bote yf he wel worche.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xvii. 219.}}
A ''witty'' man taketh preved thinge, and chaunge
He maketh, that lande from lande be not to strange.
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 64.}}
''Tamb.'' Are you the ''witty'' King of Persia?
''Myc.'' Ay, marry am I: have you any suit to me?
''Tamb.'' I would entreat you speak but three wise words.
{{right|''Marlowe'', Tamburlaine, I., ii. 4.}}
The deep, revolving, ''witty'' Buckingham.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 2. 42.}}
Upon each shoulder sits a milk-white dove,
And at her feet do ''witty'' serpents move.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', The Barriers.}}</poem>}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''2†.''' Exhibiting intelligence or ingenuity; clever; skilfully devised.
{{smaller block|<poem>Silence in love betrays more wo
{{gap}}Than words, though ne’er so ''witty;''
A beggar that is dumb, you know,
{{gap}}May challenge double pity.</poem>
{{right|''Raleigh'', Silent Lover (Ellis’s Specimens, II. 224).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ingrateful payer of my industries,
That with a soft painted hypocrisy
Cozen’st and jeer’st my perturbation,
Expect a ''witty'' and a fell revenge!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Amongst the elder Christians, some . . . in ''witty'' torments excelled the cruelty of many of their persecutors, whose rage determined quickly in death.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 91.}}}}

'''3.''' Possessed of wit; smartly or cleverly facetious; ready with strikingly novel, clever, shrewd, and amusing sayings, or with sharp repartee; brilliant, sparkling, and original in expressing amusing notions or ideas; hence, sometimes, sarcastic; satirical: of persons.
{{smaller block|<poem>Who so in earnest vveenes, he doth, in mine aduise,
Shevv himselfe vvitless, or more ''vvittie'' than vvise.</poem>
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 170.}}}}
{{smaller block|Sir Ellis Layton, whom I find a wonderful ''witty'', ready man for sudden answers and little tales, and sayings very extraordinary witty.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, III. 92.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In gentle Verse the ''Witty'' told their Flame,
And grac’d their choicest Song with Emma’s Name.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Henry and Emma.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|Honeycomb, who was so unmercifully ''witty'' upon the women, . . . has given the ladies ample satisfaction by marrying a farmer’s daughter.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 530.}}}}
'''4.''' Characterized by or pregnant with wit: as, a ''witty'' remark or repartee.
{{smaller block|<poem>Or rhymes or sangs he’d mak’ himsel’,
Or ''witty'' catches.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', To J. Lapraik, i.}}}}

'''witwal<sup>1</sup>''' (wit′wâl), ''n.'' [Also ''witwall'', and formerly assimilated ''wittal''; also erroneously ''whitwall''; a var. of ''woodwal'', ''woodwale'': see ''woodwale'', and cf. ''wittol''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' The popinjay, or green woodpecker, ''Gecinus viridis''. See ''woodwale'', and cut under ''popinjay''.
{{smaller block|<poem>No sound was heard, except, from far away,
The ringing of the ''Whitwall’s'' shrilly laughter,
Or, now and then, the chatter of the jay,
That Echo murmur’d after.</poem>
{{right|''Hood'', Haunted House, i.}}}}
'''2.''' The greater spotted woodpecker, ''Picus major''. See cut under ''Picus''.

'''witwal<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' See ''wittol''<sup>1</sup>.

'''witwanton†''' (wit′won″to̤n), ''n.'' [< ''wit''<sup>1</sup> + ''wanton''.] One who indulges in idle, foolish, and irreverent fancies or speculations. Also used adjectively.
{{smaller block|All Epicures, ''Wit-wantons'', Athëists.
{{right|''Sylvester'', Lacrymæ Lacrymarum.}}
How dangerous it is for ''wit-wanton'' men to dance with their nice distinctions on such mystical precipices.
{{right|''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., X. iv. 4.}}}}

'''witwanton†''' (wit′won″to̤n), ''v. i.'' [< ''witwanton'', ''n.''] To indulge in vain, sportive, or over-subtle fancies; speculate idly or irreverently: with an indefinite ''it''.
readings.c3s2:
{{smaller block|Dangerous it is to ''witwanton it'' with the majesty of God.
{{right|''Fuller'', Holy State.}}}}

'''wit-worm†''' (wit′wėrm), ''n.'' [< ''wit''<sup>1</sup> + ''worm''.] One who has developed into a wit. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>''Ful.'' What hast thou done
With thy poor innocent self?
''Gal.'' Wherefore, sweet madam?
''Ful.'' Thus to come forth, so suddenly, a ''witworm?''</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, ii. 1.}}}}

'''wive''' (wīv), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wived'', ppr. ''wiving''. [< ME. ''wiven'', < AS. ''wīfian'' (= MD. ''wijven'' = MLG. ''wiven''), take a wife, < ''wīf'', wife. Cf. ''wife'', ''v.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To take a wife; marry.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hanging and ''wiving'' goes by destiny.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 9. 83.}}
A shrewd wife brings thee bate, ''wiue'' not and neuer thriue. ''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 171.}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To match to a wife; provide with a wife.
{{smaller block|An I could get me but a wife, . . . I were manned, horsed, and ''wived''. ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 2. 61.

Gregory VII. . . . determined . . . that no ''wived'' priest should celebrate or even assist at the Mass.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', V. 293.}}}}
'''2.''' To take for a wife; marry. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Should I ''wive'' an Empresse,
And take her dowerlesse, should we love, or hate,
In that my bounty equalls her estate.</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', Royal King (Works, ed. Pearson, 1874, VI. 79).}}
I have ''wived'' his sister. {{right|''Scott''.}}}}

'''wivehood†''' (wīv′hu̇d), ''n.'' Same as ''wifehood''.
{{smaller block|<poem>That girdle gave the vertue of chast love,
And ''wivehood'' true, to all that did it beare.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. v. 3.}}}}

'''wiveless†''' (wīv′les), ''a.'' Same as ''wifeless''.

'''witters''', ''n. pl.'' See ''withers''.

'''witticaster''' (wit′i-kas-tėr), ''n.''   [< ''witty'' + ''-c-aster'' as in ''criticaster''.]   An inferior or pretended wit.

{{smaller block|The mention of a nobleman seems quite sufficient to arouse the spleen of our ''witticaster''. {{right|''Milton.''}}}}

'''witticheniteite''' (wit′i-ken-īt), ''n.'' A sulphid of bismuth and copper, related in form and composition to bournonite. It was first found at Wittichen, Baden.

'''witticism''' (wit′i-sizm), ''n.''   [< ''witty'' + ''-c-ism'' as in ''Atticism'', ''Gallicism'', etc.]   A witty sentence, phrase, or remark; an observation characterized by wit.

{{smaller block|You have quite undone the young King with your ''Witticisms'', and ruin’d his Fortunes utterly. {{right|''Milton'', Ans. to Salmasius, iii.}}}}

{{smaller block|The witty poets . . . have taken an advantage from the doubtful meaning of the word fire to make an infinite number of ''witticisms''. {{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 62.}}}}

{{smaller block|Every ''witticism'' is an inexact thought; what is perfectly true is imperfectly witty. {{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Diogenes and Plato.}}}}

'''wittified†''' (wit′i-fīd), ''a.''   [< *''wittify'' (< ''witty'' + ''-fy'') + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Having wit; clever; witty.

{{smaller block|Diverse of these were . . . dispersed to those ''wittified'' ladies who were willing to come into the order. {{right|''Roger North'', Lord Guilford, I. 59. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''wittily''' (wit′i-li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wittily''; < ''witty'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In a witty manner. {{smaller|(''a''†) Knowingly; intelligently; ingeniously; cunningly; artfully.}}

{{smaller block|Time only & custom haue authoritie to do, specially in all cases of language, as the Poet hath ''wittily'' remembred. {{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 104.}}}}

<poem>The ''wittily'' and strangely cruel Macro.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, v. 10.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''b'') With a witty turn or phrase, or with an ingenious and amusing association of ideas; clearly; brilliantly.}}

{{smaller block|In conversation ''wittily'' pleasant. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}}
{{smaller block|It would a little cool the preternatural heat of the flingbrand fraternity, as one ''wittily'' calleth them.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 125.}}}}

'''wittiness''' (wit′i-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The character of being witty; the quality of being ingenious or clever.
{{smaller block|''Wittinesse'' in devising, . . . pithinesse in uttering.
{{right|''E. K.'', To G. Harvey (Prefixed to Spenser’s Shep. Cal.).}}}}
'''2†.''' Something that is witty; an ingenious invention.
{{smaller block|The third, in the discoloured mantle spangled all over, is Euphantaste, a well-conceited ''wittinesse'', and employed in honouring the court with the riches of her pure invention.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, v. 3.}}}}

'''witting†''' (wit′ing), ''n.''   [Also ''weeting'' (and erroneously ''wotting''); < ME. ''witinge, wetynge''; verbal n. of ''wit''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   Knowledge; perception.
{{smaller block|<poem>That were an abusyoun
That God sholde han no parfit clere ''wetynge''
More than we men, that han douteous wenynge.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 991.}}}}

'''wittingly''' (wit′ing-li), ''adv.''   [Formerly also ''weetingly''; < ME. ''witingly, wetyngly, witindeliche'' (= MHG. ''wizzentliche'' = Icel. ''vitanliga''); < ''witting'', ppr. of ''wit''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In a witting manner; knowingly; consciously; by design.
{{smaller block|He knowingly and ''wittingly'' brought evil into the world.
{{right|''Sir T. More.''}}}}
{{smaller block|To which she for his sake had ''weetingly'' now brought her selfe, and blam’d her noble blood.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. 3. 11.}}}}
437 {{smaller block|I would not ''wittingly'' dishonor my work by a single falsehood, misrepresentation, or prejudice, though it should gain our forefathers the whole country of New England. {{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 201.}}}}

'''wittol'''<sup>1</sup>† (wit′ọl), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''wittal'', ''wittall'' (also ''wittold'', with excrescent ''d'' as in ''cuckold''), orig. ''witwal'', a particular use of ''witwal'', the popinjay: see ''witwal''<sup>1</sup>. This bird was the subject of frequent ribald allusions, similar to the allusions to the cuckoo which are prominent in the English drama of Shakspere and his contemporaries and which produced the word ''cuckold''. The addition of the notion of ‘knowing’ and submitting may be due to the popular association with ''wit'', which produced the etymology < ''wit''<sup>1</sup> + ''all''.]   A man who knows his wife’s infidelity and submits to it; a submissive cuckold.
{{smaller block|Amaimon sounds well; Lucifer well; . . . yet they are . . . the names of fiends; but, Cuckold, ''Wittol'', Cuckold! the devil himself hath not such a name! {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 2. 313.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Fond ''wit-wal'', that wouldst load thy witless head
With timely horns, before thy bridal bed!</poem>
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Satires, I. vii. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|To see . . . a ''wittol'' wink at his wife’s honesty, and too perspicuous in all other affairs. {{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 44.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There was no peeping hole to clear
The ''wittal’s'' eye from his incarnate fear.</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, i. 5.}}}}

'''wittol'''<sup>1</sup>† (wit′ọl), ''v. t.''   [Also ''wittal''; < ''wittol''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   To make a wittol, or contented cuckold, of.
{{smaller block|<poem>He would ''wittal'' me
With a consent to my own horns.</poem>
{{right|''Davenport'', City Night Cap, i. 1.}}}}

''Gal.'' Wherefore, sweet madam?
''Ful.'' Thus to come forth, so suddenly, a ''witworm?''</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, ii. 1.}}}}

'''wive''' (wīv), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wived'', ppr. ''wiving''.   [< ME. ''wiven'', < AS. ''wīfian'' (= MD. ''wijven'' = MLG. ''wiven''), take a wife, < ''wīf'', wife. Cf. ''wife'', ''v.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To take a wife; marry.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hanging and ''wiving'' goes by destiny.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 9. 83.}}}}
{{smaller block|A shrewd wife brings thee bate, ''wiue'' not and neuer thriue.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 171.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To match to a wife; provide with a wife.
{{smaller block|An I could get me but a wife, . . . I were manned, horsed, and ''wived''. ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 2. 61.

Gregory VII. . . . determined . . . that no ''wived'' priest should celebrate or even assist at the Mass.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', V. 293.}}}}
'''2.''' To take for a wife; marry. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Should I ''wive'' an Empresse,
And take her dowerlesse, should we love, or hate,
In that my bounty equalls her estate.</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', Royal King (Works, ed. Pearson, 1874, VI. 79).}}}}
{{smaller block|I have ''wived'' his sister. {{right|''Scott''.}}}}

'''wivehood†''' (wīv′hu̇d), ''n.'' Same as ''wifehood''.
{{smaller block|<poem>That girdle gave the vertue of chast love,
And ''wivehood'' true, to all that did it beare.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. v. 3.}}}}

'''wiveless†''' (wīv′les), ''a.'' Same as ''wifeless''. {{smaller block|They, in their ''wiveless'' state, run into open abominations. {{right|''Homilies'', xviii. Of Matrimony.}}}}

'''wively†''' (wīv′li), ''a.'' Same as ''wifely.''
{{smaller block|''Wyuely'' loue. {{right|''J. Udall'', On 1 Cor. vii.}}}}

'''wiver†''' (wī′vėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wivere'', ''wyvere'', < OF. ''wivre'', ''givre'', a viper, < L. ''vipera'', a viper: see ''viper''. Hence ''wivern''.]   '''1.''' A serpent.
{{smaller block|<poem>Jalousye, allas! that wikked ''wyvere'',
Thus causeles is cropen into yow.</poem>{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 1010.}}}}
'''2.''' A wivern.

'''wivern''' (wī′vėrn), ''n.''   [Also ''wyvern;'' a later form, with unorig. ''-n'' as in ''bittern'', of ''wiver:'' see ''wiver''.]   In ''her.'', a monster whose fore part is that of a dragon with its fore legs and wings, while the {{img float|file=century v08 p0761 c3f1.png|width=99px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Wivern.}}}} hinder part has the form of a serpent with a barbed tail.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lakes which, when morn breaks on their quivering bed,
Blaze like a ''wyvern'' flying round the sun.</poem>{{right|''Browning'', Paracelsus.}}}}

'''wives''', ''n.'' Plural of ''wife.''
